claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 is a broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase.
claims.source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
claims.evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 3C shows Mm_bGlc17 hydrolyzes multiple substrates including TA-G, benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 is sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation.
claims.source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
claims.evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 3C shows heterologously expressed Mm_bGlc17 hydrolyzes TA-G in vitro.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 is necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
claims.source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
claims.evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4A shows that silencing Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G deglucosylation by 75% in gut extracts.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G toxicity.
claims.source: Using cross-species RNA interference, we have shown that Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G toxicity.
claims.evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4B shows that Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae have reduced growth on TA-G-containing plants compared to controls.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 is required for the preference of M. melolontha larvae for TA-G-deficient plants.
claims.source: Furthermore, Mm_bGlc17 is required for the preference of M. melolontha larvae for TA-G-deficient plants.
claims.evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4D shows that GFP-control larvae prefer TA-G-deficient plants while Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae show no preference.

claims.claim: Herbivore metabolism modulates both the toxicity and deterrence of a plant defense compound.
claims.source: Thus, herbivore metabolism modulates both the toxicity and deterrence of a plant defense compound.
claims.evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the combined findings that Mm_bGlc17 affects both larval growth (toxicity) and feeding preference (deterrence).

claims.claim: TA-G deters M. melolontha feeding.
claims.source: The most abundant latex compound, the sesquiterpene lactone glucoside taraxinic acid (TA) β-D-glucopyranosyl ester (TA-G), deters M. melolontha feeding and thereby benefits plant fitness (Huber et al., 2016a; Huber et al., 2016b; Huber et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites previous studies showing TA-G deters feeding, and Figure 4D shows control larvae avoid TA-G-containing plants.

claims.claim: TA-G benefits plant fitness.
claims.source: The most abundant latex compound, the sesquiterpene lactone glucoside taraxinic acid (TA) β-D-glucopyranosyl ester (TA-G), deters M. melolontha feeding and thereby benefits plant fitness (Huber et al., 2016a; Huber et al., 2016b; Huber et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The introduction cites previous studies demonstrating this relationship.

claims.claim: The aglycone TA was not detected in T. officinale latex.
claims.source: The aglycone TA was not detected in the latex itself but was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed larvae.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows TA is absent in latex but present in larval samples.

claims.claim: TA was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: The aglycone TA was not detected in the latex itself but was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed larvae.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows high levels of TA in regurgitant and gut samples from latex-fed larvae.

claims.claim: TA-G disappeared as soon as the latex was ingested by M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: TA-G on the other hand disappeared as soon as the latex was ingested by the larvae (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows TA-G is present in latex but absent in larval samples.

claims.claim: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) was identified in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows TA-GSH peaks in HPLC-MS analysis, and NMR data in supplementary figures confirm structure.

claims.claim: TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) was identified in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows TA-Cys peaks in HPLC-MS analysis, and NMR data in supplementary figures confirm structure.

claims.claim: The Cys sulfhydryl moiety is conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety.
claims.source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: NMR data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-6 show the chemical structure and conjugation site.

claims.claim: Lower amounts of TA-Cys-Glu and TA-Cys-Gly were present in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: Lower amounts of TA-Cys-Glu and TA-Cys-Gly were also present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows these metabolites detected in larval samples.

claims.claim: No TA-G-GSH or TA-G-Cys conjugates were detected in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
claims.source: No TA-G-GSH or TA-G-Cys conjugates were detected in this experiment.
claims.evidence: The text explicitly states these conjugates were not detected in the experiment.

claims.claim: TA is likely first conjugated to GSH and then cleaved sequentially to form other metabolites in M. melolontha.
claims.source: Based on current knowledge of the GSH pathway in insects (Schramm et al., 2012), it is likely that TA is first conjugated to GSH and then cleaved sequentially to form the other metabolites, although some conjugation to GSH prior to deglucosylation may also occur (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from known GSH pathways in insects and the metabolites detected.

claims.claim: Approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives in M. melolontha.
claims.source: Quantitative measurements showed that approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives (Figure 1D), with TA-Cys accounting for 95% of all identified compounds (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Figure 1D shows quantitative distribution of metabolites in different body parts.

claims.claim: TA-Cys accounts for 95% of all identified TA-G metabolite compounds in M. melolontha.
claims.source: Quantitative measurements showed that approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives (Figure 1D), with TA-Cys accounting for 95% of all identified compounds (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Figure 1E shows the relative proportions of different metabolites.

claims.claim: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut of M. melolontha.
claims.source: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut (Figure 1D), and this pattern was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: Figure 1D shows the highest concentration of metabolites in the anterior midgut.

claims.claim: The pattern of TA-Cys accumulation in the anterior midgut was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G.
claims.source: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut (Figure 1D), and this pattern was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 7 shows consistent distribution over time.

claims.claim: The frass of M. melolontha only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates.
claims.source: In contrast to the different body parts, the frass only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates and was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 1D-E shows very low levels of metabolites in frass.

claims.claim: The frass of M. melolontha was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G.
claims.source: In contrast to the different body parts, the frass only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates and was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 1D-E shows TA-G is the main compound in frass.

claims.claim: The deglucosylation and GSH conjugation of TA is a major route for metabolism of this sesquiterpene lactone in M. melolontha.
claims.source: Thus, the deglucosylation and GSH conjugation of TA is a major route for metabolism of this sesquiterpene lactone in M. melolontha.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the quantitative data showing 25% conversion to GSH conjugates.

claims.claim: TA-G in T. officinale latex was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4.
claims.source: TA-G in T. officinale latex incubated at different pH levels at room temperature was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4, but not at lower or higher pH values (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A shows high deglucosylation activity at pH 4.6 and 5.4.

claims.claim: TA-G in T. officinale latex was not enzymatically deglucosylated at pH values lower than 4.6 or higher than 5.4.
claims.source: TA-G in T. officinale latex incubated at different pH levels at room temperature was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4, but not at lower or higher pH values (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A shows minimal deglucosylation activity outside the pH 4.6-5.4 range.

claims.claim: The midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8.
claims.source: As the midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8 (Figure 2B; Egert et al., 2005), the deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited.
claims.evidence: Figure 2B shows pH data, and Egert et al., 2005 is cited as a reference.

claims.claim: The deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited in the M. melolontha midgut.
claims.source: As the midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8 (Figure 2B; Egert et al., 2005), the deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mismatch between plant enzyme pH optimum (4.6-5.4) and gut pH (>8).

claims.claim: Strong deglucosylation activity was detected in the proximal parts of the M. melolontha gut, especially in the anterior midgut.
claims.source: Strong deglucosylation activity was detected in the proximal parts of the gut, especially in the anterior midgut (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Figure 2B shows highest deglucosylation activity in anterior midgut extracts.

claims.claim: TA-G hydrolysis occurred when M. melolontha larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex.
claims.source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Figure 2C shows TA formation in larvae fed heat-deactivated latex.

claims.claim: Heat-deactivated T. officinale latex no longer hydrolyzes TA-G.
claims.source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A shows no deglucosylation in boiled latex samples.

claims.claim: The presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins.
claims.source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Figure 2C shows no significant difference in TA or conjugate levels between intact and heat-deactivated latex treatments.

claims.claim: Insect-derived enzymes are sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
claims.source: Therefore, insect-derived enzymes are sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing TA-G hydrolysis occurs with heat-deactivated plant enzymes.

claims.claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2 show dose-dependent inhibition by castanospermine.

claims.claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was not inhibited by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose.
claims.source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows no inhibition by acarbose.

claims.claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was not inhibited by the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate.
claims.source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows no inhibition by bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate.

claims.claim: β-glucosidases rather than carboxylesterases catalyze TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
claims.source: This suggests that β-glucosidases rather than carboxylesterases catalyze TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the inhibitor studies showing only glucosidase inhibitors are effective.

claims.claim: 19 sequences similar to β-glucosidases had an expression profile matching the observed pattern of high TA-G deglucosylation activity in the anterior midgut of M. melolontha.
claims.source: 19 sequences similar to β-glucosidases had an expression profile matching the observed pattern of high TA-G deglucosylation activity in the anterior midgut.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the transcriptome analysis.

claims.claim: 12 full-length β-glucosidases were amplified from M. melolontha cDNA sharing between 55 and 79% amino acid similarity.
claims.source: Partial sequences were extended using rapid-amplification of complementary DNA (cDNA) ends polymerase chain reaction (RACE PCR), resulting in 12 full-length β-glucosidases sharing between 55 and 79% amino acid similarity (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A shows the phylogenetic tree of the 12 β-glucosidases.

claims.claim: All amplified M. melolontha β-glucosidase sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal.
claims.source: All amplified sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal and possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Sanz-Aparicio et al., 1998; Davies and Henrissat, 1995; Barrett et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the sequence alignment with signal peptides.

claims.claim: All amplified M. melolontha β-glucosidase sequences possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases.
claims.source: All amplified sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal and possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Sanz-Aparicio et al., 1998; Davies and Henrissat, 1995; Barrett et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows these conserved motifs in the alignment.

claims.claim: Expression levels of the candidate M. melolontha β-glucosidase genes were 37- to 308-fold higher in the anterior than posterior midgut samples.
claims.source: Expression levels of the candidate genes were 37- to 308-fold higher in the anterior than posterior midgut samples (padj <10–5, exact tests, n = 3), thus matching the differences in TA-G deglucosylation rate between these gut compartments (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Figure 3B shows the heat map of expression levels in different gut sections.

claims.claim: Average expression of the M. melolontha β-glucosidase transcripts did not differ among larvae fed water, TA-G, or latex.
claims.source: Average expression of the transcripts did not differ among M. melolontha larvae fed water, TA-G, or latex (Figure 3B; padj >0.50, exact tests, n = 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 3B shows similar expression levels across different diet treatments.

claims.claim: 9 of the 12 heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside.
claims.source: 9 of the 12 β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside, and hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows activity with Glc-MU for 9 enzymes.

claims.claim: 9 of the 12 heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites tested.
claims.source: 9 of the 12 β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside, and hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows substrate specificity for different plant glycosides.

claims.claim: All tested plant glycoside substrates were deglucosylated by at least one M. melolontha glucosidase.
claims.source: All tested substrates were deglucosylated by at least one M. melolontha glucosidase (Figure 3C) in agreement with the hydrolysis activity of crude midgut extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows that each substrate column has at least one positive result.

claims.claim: Five heterologously expressed M. melolontha proteins deglucosylated TA-G.
claims.source: Five heterologously expressed proteins deglucosylated TA-G (Figure 3C), with the highest TA aglycone formation found for Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows five enzymes with TA-G activity.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 showed the highest TA aglycone formation among heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases.
claims.source: Five heterologously expressed proteins deglucosylated TA-G (Figure 3C), with the highest TA aglycone formation found for Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 4 shows Mm_bGlc17 produces the most TA.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 deglyosylated benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose in addition to TA-G.
claims.source: Apart from TA-G, Mm_bGlc17 also deglyosylated benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose.
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows Mm_bGlc17 activity with multiple substrates.

claims.claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc17 resulted in a stable and specific reduction of the target mRNA after 5 days.
claims.source: After 5 days, a stable and specific reduction of the target mRNAs had occurred (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3 show reduced Mm_bGlc17 expression in silenced larvae.

claims.claim: TA-G deglucosylation was reduced by 75% in gut extracts of M. melolontha larvae that were silenced in Mm_bGlc17.
claims.source: TA-G deglucosylation was reduced by 75% in gut extracts of larvae that were silenced in Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows significantly reduced deglucosylation activity in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae.

claims.claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to GFP controls.
claims.source: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 and Mm_bGlu18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to green fluorescent protein (GFP) controls (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows no significant difference between Mm_bGlc16-silenced and GFP control larvae.

claims.claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to GFP controls.
claims.source: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 and Mm_bGlu18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to green fluorescent protein (GFP) controls (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows no significant difference between Mm_bGlc18-silenced and GFP control larvae.

claims.claim: Mm_Glc17 accounts for most of the TA-G deglucosylation in vivo in M. melolontha.
claims.source: These results confirm that M. melolontha-derived β-glucosidases hydrolyze TA-G and demonstrate that Mm_Glc17 accounts for most of the TA-G deglucosylation in vivo.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the 75% reduction in activity when Mm_bGlc17 is silenced.

claims.claim: The interaction of Mm_bGlc17 silencing and plant genotype significantly affected M. melolontha larval growth.
claims.source: The interaction of Mm_bGlc17 silencing and plant genotype significantly affected larval growth (Figure 4B; p(Mm_bGlc17 x TA-G) = 0.009, two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows the statistical interaction between enzyme silencing and plant genotype on growth.

claims.claim: On TA-G-containing plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing reduced M. melolontha larval growth.
claims.source: On TA-G-containing plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing reduced larval growth, with GFP-control larvae gaining 4.5% body weight and Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae losing 1.4% body weight (Figure 4B; p = 0.009, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows reduced weight gain in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae on wild-type plants.

claims.claim: On TA-G-deficient plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not affect M. melolontha larval weight gain.
claims.source: By contrast, on TA-G-deficient plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not affect larval weight gain (p = 0.19, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows no significant difference in growth on TA-G-deficient plants.

claims.claim: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants.
claims.source: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants (p = 0.035, Student's t-test; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), while the reversed pattern was found in tendency for Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae (p = 0.099, Student's t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 show this growth pattern.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17-silenced M. melolontha larvae showed a tendency for lower growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants.
claims.source: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants (p = 0.035, Student's t-test; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), while the reversed pattern was found in tendency for Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae (p = 0.099, Student's t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 4 shows this trend.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants.
claims.source: Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants (Figure 4C; p = 0.04, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4C shows higher Mm_bGlc17 expression on wild-type plants.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 expression is induced by TA-G.
claims.source: As Mm_bGlc17 benefited larval growth in the presence of TA-G, we investigated whether the expression of this gene is induced by TA-G. Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants (Figure 4C; p = 0.04, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4C shows increased expression in the presence of TA-G.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 increases M. melolontha larval performance in the presence of TA-G.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that Mm_bGlc17 expression is induced by TA-G and increases larval performance in the presence of TA-G.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the growth data showing Mm_bGlc17 benefits larvae on TA-G-containing plants.

claims.claim: GFP-silenced control M. melolontha larvae were deterred by TA-G.
claims.source: GFP-silenced control larvae were deterred by TA-G, with over 60% of the larvae feeding on TA-G-deficient plants and 30-% on the wild-type (Figure 4D; p(3h) = 0.006, binomial test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4D shows GFP-control larvae preferentially chose TA-G-deficient plants.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17-silenced M. melolontha larvae did not show any preference for TA-G-deficient over TA-G-producing wild-type plants.
claims.source: By contrast, Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae did not show any preference for TA-G-deficient over TA-G-producing wild-type plants: 44% of the larvae fed on wild-type plants, while 42% fed on TA-G-deficient plants (Figure 4D; p(3h) = 0.86, binomial test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4D shows no significant preference in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae.

claims.claim: The choice patterns of M. melolontha larvae between TA-G-deficient and wild-type plants were constant over time.
claims.source: Both patterns were constant over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 6 shows stable choice patterns over 4 hours.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not significantly affect the total percentage of M. melolontha larvae that made a choice.
claims.source: Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not significantly affect the total percentage of larvae that made a choice (86% Mm_bGlc17 vs 91% GFP).
claims.evidence: The text provides the percentages showing similar choice rates.

claims.claim: Mm_bGlc17 expression is required for the deterrent effect of TA-G toward M. melolontha.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that Mm_bGlc17 expression is required for the deterrent effect of TA-G toward M. melolontha.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the choice experiment showing loss of deterrence when Mm_bGlc17 is silenced.

claims.claim: A major metabolization product of TA-G is TA-Cys, with about 25% of the ingested TA-G accumulating in this form.
claims.source: A major metabolization product of TA-G is TA-Cys, with about 25% of the ingested TA-G accumulating in this form.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the quantitative data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: It is likely that TA-G is deglucosylated prior conjugation to GSH and subsequently sequentially cleaved to TA-Cys by peptidases.
claims.source: Based on our current knowledge of the GSH pathway in insects (Schramm et al., 2012), it is likely that TA-G is deglucosylated prior conjugation to GSH and subsequently sequentially cleaved to TA-Cys by peptidases.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from known GSH pathways and the metabolites detected.

claims.claim: The first step of TA-G metabolization, the conjugation of GSH to TA, may occur spontaneously and/or via GSH glucosyl-transferases.
claims.source: The first step of this metabolization pathway, the conjugation of GSH to TA, may occur spontaneously and/or via GSH glucosyl-transferases.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the chemistry of the reaction.

claims.claim: When TA and TA-G were incubated with high concentrations of GSH and Cys in vitro, several isomers of the conjugates formed that were not detected inside the M. melolontha gut.
claims.source: When we incubated TA and TA-G with high concentrations of GSH and Cys in vitro, several isomers of the conjugates formed that were not detected inside the M. melolontha gut, suggesting that enzymatic rather than spontaneous conjugation of GSH to TA prevails inside the larva.

results.result: TA-G is rapidly deglucosylated in the M. melolontha gut, with TA-G disappearing upon ingestion and TA appearing in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C13 are supported by Figure 1A showing TA-G present in latex but absent in larval samples, while TA is absent in latex but present in high levels in regurgitant and gut samples. The data directly demonstrate rapid deglucosylation upon ingestion.

results.result: TA-G is conjugated to glutathione in M. melolontha, with approximately 25% of ingested TA-G converted to GSH conjugates (primarily TA-Cys, 95% of identified compounds), which accumulate mainly in the anterior midgut.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C14-C26, C70 are supported by HPLC-MS and NMR data (Figures 1B-E and supplements) identifying TA-GSH, TA-Cys, and other conjugates, with quantitative measurements showing distribution patterns. The structural characterization via NMR and mass spectrometry provides strong evidence for GSH conjugation.

results.result: Plant-derived TA-G hydrolases have an acidic pH optimum (4.6-5.4) and are likely inhibited in the alkaline M. melolontha midgut (pH >8).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30, C93-C94 are supported by Figure 2A showing pH-dependent deglucosylation activity of plant enzymes, with optimal activity at pH 4.6-5.4 and minimal activity at pH 8. Figure 2B confirms gut pH >8, supporting the inference that plant enzymes are inhibited in vivo.

results.result: Insect-derived enzymes are sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha, as demonstrated by deglucosylation activity in gut extracts and in larvae fed heat-deactivated latex.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35, C95, C99 are supported by Figure 2B showing high deglucosylation activity in anterior midgut extracts, and Figure 2C showing TA formation in larvae fed heat-deactivated latex with no difference compared to intact latex. This provides strong evidence that insect enzymes alone are sufficient.

results.result: β-glucosidases rather than carboxylesterases catalyze TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha, as shown by inhibitor studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 are supported by Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2 showing dose-dependent inhibition by the β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate. The differential inhibition pattern provides strong evidence for β-glucosidase activity.

results.result: Twelve full-length β-glucosidases were identified from M. melolontha with characteristic glucosidase motifs and expression patterns matching TA-G deglucosylation activity (37-308 fold higher in anterior vs posterior midgut).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by transcriptome analysis and Figure 3A-B showing phylogenetic relationships, conserved motifs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and expression patterns matching enzymatic activity. The molecular characterization is thorough and well-documented.

results.result: Nine of twelve heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases showed activity, with five deglucosylating TA-G. Mm_bGlc17 showed the highest TA-G activity and is a broad-spectrum enzyme hydrolyzing multiple substrates including benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C46-C51 are supported by Figure 3C and supplements showing substrate specificity of heterologously expressed enzymes. Mm_bGlc17 demonstrates broad substrate specificity with highest TA-G activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The in vitro characterization is comprehensive.

results.result: Mm_bGlc17 is necessary for TA-G deglucosylation in vivo, as silencing reduced deglucosylation activity by 75% in gut extracts, while silencing Mm_bGlc16 or Mm_bGlc18 had no significant effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C52-C56, C97 are supported by Figure 4A showing 75% reduction in TA-G deglucosylation in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae with stable and specific knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3). The RNAi specificity controls strengthen the conclusion that Mm_bGlc17 accounts for most in vivo activity.

results.result: Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G toxicity and increases larval performance on TA-G-containing plants. Silencing Mm_bGlc17 reduced growth on TA-G-containing plants but not on TA-G-deficient plants, suggesting deglucosylation reduces rather than enhances toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C57-C61, C64, C103-C104 are supported by Figure 4B showing significant interaction between Mm_bGlc17 silencing and plant genotype (p=0.009), with reduced growth in silenced larvae only on TA-G-containing plants. The experiment was replicated (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Mm_bGlc17 expression is induced by TA-G, increasing by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by Figure 4C showing statistically significant (p=0.04) increased Mm_bGlc17 expression on wild-type plants. However, the authors note this contradicts initial RNA-seq results (C45), suggesting context-dependent regulation that requires further investigation.

results.result: Mm_bGlc17 is required for the deterrent effect of TA-G, as GFP-control larvae avoided TA-G-containing plants (60% preference for TA-G-deficient) while Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae showed no preference (44% vs 42%).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C65-C69, C98 are supported by Figure 4D showing statistically significant preference in GFP controls (p=0.006) but not in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae (p=0.86). The choice patterns were stable over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), and silencing did not affect overall choice behavior (86% vs 91%), indicating specific loss of TA-G deterrence.

results.result: Herbivore metabolism modulates both toxicity and deterrence of TA-G, with the insect β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17 mediating both effects and potentially shaping plant defense evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C80, C86, C88 integrate findings from growth (C57-C61) and choice experiments (C65-C69) to conclude that Mm_bGlc17 affects both toxicity and deterrence. This synthesis is well-supported by the combined experimental evidence, though the evolutionary implications remain speculative.

results.result: TA-G is likely deglucosylated prior to GSH conjugation, with enzymatic rather than spontaneous conjugation prevailing in vivo. TA-Cys must be further metabolized to unknown products given low excretion despite accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are inferred from metabolite profiles and known GSH pathways but lack direct experimental evidence. The observation of different conjugate isomers in vitro vs in vivo (C73) suggests enzymatic specificity, but the proposed metabolic pathway and fate of TA-Cys remain speculative and require additional experiments.

results.result: The deglucosylation of TA-G depends primarily on β-glucosidases from M. melolontha rather than plant enzymes, as demonstrated by multiple lines of evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C96 synthesize evidence from pH studies (C27-C30), gut extract activity (C31-C35), heat-deactivation experiments (C32-C34), in vitro enzyme characterization (C46-C51), and RNAi knockdown (C52-C56). The convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: Deglycosylation of TA-G may reduce toxicity through multiple mechanisms: faster GSH conjugation of TA than TA-G, blocking activity in hydrophilic compartments, or enhanced nutritional quality from liberated glucose.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 propose mechanistic explanations for reduced toxicity but are entirely speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION). No experimental data directly test these hypotheses. While the proposals are reasonable, they require experimental validation to be considered supported.

results.result: TA-G recognition through deglucosylation may guide larvae to nutritious feeding sites (side roots with lower TA-G and higher protein) rather than reflecting toxicity avoidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 propose an alternative explanation for deterrence behavior based on cited observations about root preferences (C111-C112). However, this remains speculative as no experiments directly test whether larvae use TA-G as a nutritional cue. The hypothesis is plausible but unsupported by current data.

results.result: Herbivore growth may give an incomplete picture of TA-G costs, as metabolism could deplete cysteine or increase mortality under natural conditions, potentially explaining avoidance despite improved growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 propose that growth alone doesn't capture fitness costs, citing examples from other systems (C115-C116). While conceptually valid, these remain speculative explanations for the counterintuitive results. No data directly test cysteine depletion or mortality effects in this system.

results.result: Mm_bGlc17 may be maintained for nutrient acquisition (cellobiose hydrolysis suggests digestive origin), with dandelions exploiting this promiscuous enzyme constrained by primary functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119, C121 propose an evolutionary scenario based on Mm_bGlc17's broad substrate specificity including cellobiose (C51, C121). While the cellobiose activity suggests digestive origin, the evolutionary constraint hypothesis is speculative and requires comparative or experimental evolution studies to test.

results.result: The broad substrate specificity of Mm_bGlc17 is unusual, and the diversity of β-glucosidases in insect herbivores suggests plant defenses play an underestimated role in their evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C120, C122-C123 are supported by the demonstrated broad specificity of Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 3C) and cited literature on β-glucosidase diversity and phylogenetic patterns. The inference about evolutionary importance is reasonable given the species-specific clustering and large number of β-glucosidases in herbivores.

results.result: TA-G deters M. melolontha feeding and benefits plant fitness, with high M. melolontha pressure selecting for high TA-G genotypes in dandelions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C81-C83 are supported by citations to previous work (Huber et al., 2016a,b, 2015) and confirmed by current choice experiments (Figure 4D) showing GFP-control larvae avoid TA-G-containing plants.
